lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: be able to use chemical equations to calculate volumes of gases and vice versa, using: i the concepts of amount of substance ii the molar volume of gases iii the expression pV = n RT for gases and volatile liquids

primer.text: Gases are the forgiving state: any mole of any gas claims the same volume. This note fixes the 24.0 dm3 room-condition and 22.4 dm3 standard-condition values, chains gas volumes through equation ratios, then extends to any conditions with the ideal gas expression pV = nRT and its SI unit discipline.

modules.title: Molar gas volumes
modules.opening: Under the same conditions, one mole of any gas claims the same volume. This lesson pins the 24.0 dm^3 r.t.p. and 22.4 dm^3 s.t.p. values, converts volumes to moles and back, and chains gas volumes through equation ratios.
keyPoints: At r.t.p. (293 K, 101.3 kPa) the molar gas volume is 24.0 dm^3; at s.t.p. (273 K) it is 22.4 dm^3.
Moles of gas = volume in dm^3 / molar gas volume.
Gas volumes scale with equation ratios: 6.50 dm^3 of propane yields 45.5 dm^3 of total gaseous products.
Volume foresight sizes the equipment for gas-evolving experiments.

low.restatement: Divide the gas volume by 24.0 (room conditions) to get moles, or multiply moles by 24.0 to predict the volume.
low.analogy: Every gas fills a same-sized apartment at room conditions; moles count apartments occupied.
low.examPointer: State which conditions you are using - the 24.0 vs 22.4 choice is itself a mark.

medium.restatement: Because equal volumes hold equal numbers of gas particles (Avogadro's law), the equation's mole ratio applies directly to volumes at fixed temperature and pressure, even between different gases.
medium.analogy: Gas volumes behave like identical train carriages: the ratio of carriages needed is the ratio written in the equation.
medium.examPointer: For propane C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O (steam), each 1 volume of propane gives 7 volumes of gaseous product - 6.50 x 7 = 45.5 dm^3.

modules.title: The ideal gas expression
modules.opening: Away from room conditions, pV = nRT takes over. This lesson states the kinetic theory assumptions behind 'ideal', fixes the SI unit discipline (Pa, m^3, K), and extracts both volumes and molar masses from the expression.
keyPoints: Ideal gases follow kinetic theory: fast random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions.
pV = nRT uses pressure in Pa, volume in m^3, temperature in K, and R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1.
Rearranging gives volumes (V = nRT/p) or moles (n = pV/RT) or molar masses.
kPa multiply by 1000 for Pa; cm^3 divide by 10^6 for m^3; Celsius add 273 for K.

low.restatement: Pressure times volume equals moles times gas constant times temperature; three of the four quantities decide the fourth.
low.analogy: It is a four-way seesaw: squeeze the volume and the pressure rises; heat it and either pressure or volume must grow.
low.examPointer: The Data Booklet supplies R; your job is the SI conversions and the rearrangement.

medium.restatement: The expression derives from kinetic theory: particle impacts create pressure, so pV scales with the particle count n and their average kinetic energy, which temperature measures.
medium.analogy: Pressure is the drumbeat of molecules on the walls - more molecules (n) or faster ones (T) beat louder (p).
medium.examPointer: Real gases only approximate ideal behaviour; exam data are chosen so the deviation is negligible.

glossary.definition: The volume one mole of any gas occupies at stated conditions: 24.0 dm^3 at r.t.p., 22.4 dm^3 at s.t.p.
A gas obeying the kinetic theory assumptions and pV = nRT exactly.
The model of fast, randomly moving, volume-less particles colliding elastically, with temperature measuring average kinetic energy.

workedExample.prompt: Find the volume that 0.781 mol of oxygen claims at 220 kPa and 21 degrees C.
steps: Convert: 220 kPa = 220000 Pa; 21 degrees C = 294 K.
